prompt: Your team practises trunk-based development (merge at least daily). You need to build a new recommendations engine that will take three weeks before it is usable. What is the standard approach?

options.text: Make an exception: keep a three-week branch and merge it at the end
options.explanation: That reintroduces exactly the late, large integration TBD is designed to avoid, with three weeks of drift from everyone else's changes.

options.text: Develop in a fork and copy the files across when done
options.explanation: A fork is just a long-lived branch in another repository, with all the same integration costs and less visibility.

options.text: Freeze trunk for three weeks while the feature is built
options.explanation: A code freeze blocks everyone else's work and is a symptom TBD tries to eliminate, not a tool it uses.

options.text: Merge small slices to trunk daily, with the feature hidden behind a feature flag that stays off until it is ready
options.explanation: Correct. Keep unfinished behavior gated, maintain compatible initialisation and schema migrations, and test both intended paths. Gating with a feature flag does not by itself prove the deployment safe.

workedExample:
1. Day 1: add the flag `recs_v2` (default off) and a stub behind it. Merge.
2. Days 2-14: build the engine in small PRs. Each merges to trunk; CI runs the new code's tests; the gated behaviour stays hidden while compatible initialisation and data changes keep the existing path working.
3. Day 15: enable for internal staff, then 1% of users, then everyone.
4. Day 20: delete the flag and the old code path.

If the new engine replaces an existing component, use branch by abstraction: put an interface in front of the old one, migrate callers, then swap implementations behind it.

link.title: Feature Toggles — Pete Hodgson on martinfowler.com

prompt: A team keeps 14 active long-lived branches, merges each into trunk about once a fortnight, and holds a two-week code freeze before every release. Releases are slow and painful. Which changes move it towards the practices DORA's trunk-based development research associated with higher delivery performance? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reduce to three or fewer active branches
options.explanation: Correct. DORA's analysis associated three or fewer active branches with higher delivery performance.

options.text: Merge into trunk at least daily, using feature flags or branch by abstraction for unfinished work
options.explanation: Correct. Daily merging to trunk is the defining habit, and flags or branch by abstraction make it safe for incomplete features.

options.text: Lengthen the code freeze to four weeks so integration has more time
options.explanation: Incorrect. DORA lists having no code freezes and no integration phases as part of the high-performing pattern; a longer freeze moves further from it.

options.text: Add a separate long-lived integration branch where features wait before reaching trunk
options.explanation: Incorrect. An extra integration branch (like GitFlow's `develop`) is a second place to integrate, which works against merging into trunk daily.

options.text: Replace the freeze and integration phase with continuous integration on trunk
options.explanation: Correct. When trunk is integrated and tested continuously, there is no big integration phase left to freeze for.

workedExample:
DORA's trunk-based development capability page (from its 2016 and 2017 data) lists three practices linked to better delivery performance:

1. Three or fewer active branches.
2. Merge to trunk at least daily.
3. No code freezes and no integration phases.

Compare the team with each: 14 branches, fortnightly merges and a freeze all point the wrong way. Options A, B and E move towards the pattern. A longer freeze or an extra long-lived integration branch moves away from it. These are associations from survey data, so expect them to help rather than guarantee faster delivery.

prompt: A team has used feature flags with trunk-based development for two years and now has 300 flags. Which concerns are well founded? Select all that apply.

options.text: Independent on/off flags multiply the possible configurations (each extra flag can double them), making exhaustive coverage expensive as flags accumulate
options.explanation: Ten independent flags permit 1,024 combinations. Constraints can reduce reachable combinations; whether all are tested is a property of the suite.

options.text: Old flags that are always on still carry dead code paths that can be reactivated by accident
options.explanation: Correct. The SEC described a repurposed flag invoking old Power Peg code on one server and losses exceeding $460 million in the Knight Capital incident.
Incorrect. Flags are what make daily integration of unfinished work possible; the issue is cleaning them up afterwards.

options.text: Each release flag should have an owner and an expiry, and be removed once the feature is fully rolled out
options.explanation: Correct. Treat release flags as temporary debt. Long-lived operational flags and flags that control permissions are a separate category and should be managed deliberately.

workedExample:
Weigh each concern:

1. Combinatorics: each independent on/off flag in the same flow can double the configurations (10 such flags allow 1,024), so an accumulating cluster of interacting flags can make exhaustive testing expensive.
2. Dead paths: with a flag left on for a year, its else branch goes unexercised in production (automated tests may still cover it), yet that code is still deployed and can be switched back on.
3. Flags do not block CI: they enable it.
4. Hygiene: inventory flags, tag them by type (release, experiment, operations, access control), set expiry dates, and add a lint or dashboard that flags stale ones.
